title: A Matter of Interest: Understanding Interestingness Judgments of Math Problems in Humans and Language Models
claim: We compare human and model judgments on the same inputs at matched stages, and each comparison maps to a research question.
layout: Single panel, left-to-right; stacked human and LLM lanes joined by compare arrows
description: A math problem in a blue box on the left, introduced by the text 'Given a math problem…', splits into two parallel lanes inside a large rounded grey container titled 'Is the problem interesting?'. The top lane is for humans, with person icons. It has a solid green thought cloud holding a sample rationale, which feeds a 'Compute interestingness score' box. That box branches to a 'Yes!' arrow into a blue 'Human Solution' box and a 'No…' arrow into a trash can. The bottom lane is for the LLM, with a network icon. It has the same layout in dashed outlines, with a '?' in the cloud, and ends in a blue 'LLM Solution' box. Large yellow double-headed 'compare' arrows link the two lanes, labeled RQ1 for the scores and RQ3 for the rationales. Purple RQ2a and RQ2b labels sit next to the human and LLM icons.
caption: Our experimental pipeline for studying human-LLM alignment on interestingness is depicted above. For any problem, human participants rate how interesting it is and why they find it interesting (top panel). We also evaluate LLMs' ratings for these (bottom panel), comparing human-LLM alignment on how interesting a problem is (RQ1) and their rationales for interestingness (RQ3). We explore whether the distributions of judgments between humans and LLMs align (RQ2a) and if model pooling can improve this alignment (RQ2b). While not depicted in the figure, we also study how reasoning models reason about problem interestingness (RQ4) and explore whether LLMs are capable of generating mathematical problems that interest humans (RQ5).
abstract: The evolution of mathematics is shaped importantly by interestingness: researchers choose which problems to pursue, and students choose which problems to engage with, based on expectations of interest and challenge. As AI systems, particularly large language models (LLMs) that operate flexibly over natural language and formal mathematics, are increasingly used in mathematics research and education, it becomes crucial to characterize how closely their judgments align with people from different mathematical backgrounds. We study whether LLMs align with human interestingness judgments by comparing LLM ratings with those of two populations, crowdsourced participants with college math experience and International Math Olympiad competitors. Although many LLMs broadly agree with human notions of interestingness, they largely fail to match the distribution of human judgments. They also weakly align with why humans find problems interesting, with low correlation to human-selected rationales. Finally, we evaluate LLMs' ability to generate interesting problems and find that, after filtering for validity, LLMs are able to generate engaging problems. We conclude with takeaways, including the need for multi-LLM human-AI collaborative systems, that highlight both the promise and current limits of LLMs as partners in mathematical reasoning.
